options: A model that has only been pre-trained, so it continues text instead of answering
The smallest version of a chatbot
A model that only works offline
A model trained only on questions and answers
questions.explanation: Pre-training teaches a model to continue text. Until it's fine-tuned, that's all it does, which is why GPT-2 carried on writing instead of answering.

questions.prompt: You ask a base model "How do I make masala chai?" and it replies with three more questions about tea. Why?
options: It doesn't know anything about tea
Its context window is full
In text like the kind it learned from, a question is often followed by more questions, such as in a FAQ list
It's been told to be unhelpful
questions.explanation: A base model writes whatever plausibly comes next. Questions on the internet are often followed by more questions, so that's a likely continuation, even though it isn't what you wanted.

questions.prompt: In supervised fine-tuning, what does the model learn from?
options: Trillions of tokens from the whole internet
Example prompts with ideal answers written by people
Its own answers, with no help
A list of banned words
questions.explanation: People write prompts and the answers they'd like to see, and the model is trained on them with the same loop as pre-training. InstructGPT used about 13,000 prompts.

questions.prompt: In Llama 3.1's chat format, what does the special token <|eot_id|> do?
options: It marks the start of the user's message
It turns the model off
It hides the system message
It marks the end of a turn, so the model knows to stop after its answer
questions.explanation: Special tokens mark who says what. After fine-tuning, the model writes its answer and then <|eot_id|>, "end of turn", instead of carrying on with your next question.

questions.prompt: Why do companies collect comparisons (which of two answers is better) instead of only written answers?
options: People can judge which answer is better much faster than they can write a perfect one
Comparisons don't need any people at all
Written answers aren't allowed in training
Comparisons add new facts to the model
questions.explanation: Writing ideal answers is slow; ranking a few answers is quick. With RLHF or newer methods like DPO, the model is nudged towards the kind of answer people rank higher.

questions.prompt: People preferred a 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT model to the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 base model. What does that show?
options: Smaller models always know more
GPT-3 was badly pre-trained
How a model is trained to behave can matter more to people than its size
Parameters don't matter at all
questions.explanation: GPT-3 knew a lot but only continued text. A model over 100 times smaller, fine-tuned to follow instructions, gave answers people found more useful.

questions.prompt: A company wants its chatbot to know about products it launched last week. Is fine-tuning the best tool?
options: Yes: fine-tuning is the main way models learn facts
No: fine-tuning mostly shapes behaviour, so RAG, which hands the model the right documents, usually suits new facts better
Yes: a single example is enough to teach any fact
No: chatbots can never learn anything new
questions.explanation: The LIMA study argued that almost all a model's knowledge comes from pre-training, and fine-tuning teaches style and format. For fresh or private information, RAG (lesson 8) is usually the better choice.

questions.prompt: A chatbot warmly agrees with your plan to put all your savings into one stock. What should you take from that?
options: The plan must be good, since the AI agrees
Nothing: the chatbot is always neutral
That the stock will go up
Not much: assistants are trained partly on what people like to hear, so ask for the other side and check the facts
questions.explanation: Learning from human preferences can make models too agreeable. OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update in 2025 for being "overly flattering or agreeable". Agreement isn't evidence.
